prediction:
1) Transsphenoidal (basal) encephalocele — Most likely. Persistent craniopharyngeal canal + abnormal/small sella + tissue extending into the canal and an associated morning-glory disc favor a small communicating basal encephalocele presenting as a nasopharyngeal soft-tissue nodule. Important because biopsy/biopsy-like manipulation could cause CSF leak or infection.

2) Ectopic pituitary tissue / Rathke pouch remnant (ectopic adenohypophysis) — High likelihood. Embryologic remnant along a persistent craniopharyngeal canal can form a small solid, minimally enhancing mass in the nasopharynx; normal endocrine panel makes a functioning ectopic adenohypophysis less likely but does not exclude ectopic tissue.

3) Noncommunicating nasal glioma (heterotopic brain tissue) — Possible. Imaging may show a solid intranasal/intrapharyngeal glioma without intracranial communication; clinical overlap with small encephalocele but distinguished by lack of continuity on targeted imaging.

4) Tornwaldt (nasopharyngeal) cyst or other benign nasopharyngeal mucosal cyst — Less likely because the lesion is described as solid and minimally enhancing rather than cystic, but still a consideration for small midline lesions.

5) Congenital neoplasm (e.g., small nasopharyngeal teratoma/epignathus) or early malignancy (rhabdomyosarcoma) — Least likely given the very small size (5 mm), lack of symptoms, and benign-appearing MRI, but should remain in the differential until targeted imaging excludes other possibilities.

Recommended next steps (urgent priorities)
- Defer any biopsy or transnasal manipulation until intracranial communication is excluded.
- Obtain dedicated high-resolution skull-base MRI sequences (thin-slice sagittal and coronal T2 and steady-state/CISS or FIESTA) and contrast-enhanced pituitary protocol images to evaluate for continuity with intracranial CSF/brain and to better characterize tissue.
- Consider noncontrast CT of the skull base to define the bony craniopharyngeal canal and any defect.
- ENT and pediatric neurosurgery consultation before any invasive procedure; pediatric endocrinology follow-up for surveillance given sellar abnormality.
- If imaging confirms noncommunicating lesion and malignancy remains a concern, plan biopsy/excision in coordinated fashion with neurosurgery/ENT.
